title: Generalised abdominal pain and fever in a man with untreated cirrhosis
desc: This station involves a focused history and examination of a 45-year-old lawyer in the ED. He has had generalised abdominal pain and fever since yesterday, after two weeks of worsening abdominal swelling, jaundice, itch and bruising. He has alcohol-related cirrhosis with no follow-up and still drinks heavily. The candidate then interprets his observations, blood results and a diagnostic ascitic tap, gives the diagnosis and differentials, outlines emergency management, answers his questions about his liver and his work, and safety-nets.
focus: Fever and abdominal pain in decompensated cirrhosis: recognising and managing spontaneous bacterial peritonitis with sepsis
context: Chronic liver disease lost to follow-up
diagnosis: Sepsis with presumed acute kidney injury
stem: You are an intern working in the Emergency Department of a metropolitan hospital. Roger Lee, a 45-year-old lawyer, has come in with abdominal pain. He is in an acute bay. A nurse is with you, will tell you his observations when you ask, and will carry out any instructions you give.
tasks: Take a focused history from Roger and perform a focused examination, telling the examiner what you are examining. Give the nurse any immediate instructions you need to (10 minutes).

The examiner will give you Roger's observations, his blood results and the results of a diagnostic ascitic tap. Interpret them, give your most likely diagnosis and differentials, then outline your management approach and safety netting, and answer Roger's questions (5 minutes).
patient:
Role: You are Roger Lee, a 45-year-old lawyer. You lie on the trolley looking a little yellow and flushed, now and then scratching your arms. You are alert, articulate and a bit impatient: you want this sorted so you can get back to work. When asked about alcohol you are honest about the amount but get defensive (“it's part of my job”), then admit you feel guilty about it. Give details only when you are asked. The examiner gives examination findings from the Exam findings below when the candidate says what they are examining.

Opening line: “I've been having some terrible abdominal pain, doc.”

If asked to say more: “It was there when I woke up yesterday and has continued to get worse.”

The pain (give only when asked)

  • Site: all over your tummy (you wave a hand over the whole abdomen). It doesn't go anywhere else.
  • Onset: it came on gradually. It was there when you woke up yesterday morning.
  • Character: a constant ache. It does not come and go in waves.
  • Aggravating and relieving: worse when you press on your tummy. Nothing makes it better. You haven't taken anything for it.
  • Severity: 4 out of 10 at first, now 5 out of 10.
  • Impact: “I can't focus on anything.” You couldn't work yesterday afternoon.

Other symptoms (only when asked about each)

  • Fevers, chills and night sweats since yesterday. You soaked the sheets last night.
  • Your tummy has been swelling up over the past 2 weeks and it keeps getting bigger. Your trousers no longer do up.
  • For about 2 weeks your skin and eyes have looked yellow and your urine has been dark, “like tea”.
  • You are itchy all over.
  • You bruise very easily, especially on your arms.
  • Your appetite is a bit down. No vomiting.

Negatives (only if asked about each)

  • No confusion, drowsiness or muddled thinking. You live alone, but no-one at work has said anything and you feel “sharp as ever”.
  • No vomiting blood. No black, tarry or bloody bowel motions.
  • No pain in the upper middle of the tummy going through to the back.
  • Bowels opened normally yesterday and you are passing wind. No change in your bowel habit. No blood from the back passage. No weight loss that you know of (you have got bigger round the middle).
  • No burning indigestion or reflux. No pain after fatty meals.
  • No chest pain, palpitations, breathlessness or cough.
  • No pain or burning passing urine and no frequency.

Past history, medicines and allergies

  • Two years ago you were told you have cirrhosis of the liver. You were meant to see a liver specialist but never went, and you have had no follow-up. “I rarely see doctors.”
  • No operations on your tummy. As far as you know you don't have hepatitis. If asked about risks: no injecting drugs, no tattoos, no blood transfusions.
  • Medicines: Panadol (paracetamol) every other day for headaches. No anti-inflammatories, no other medicines, no supplements.
  • No known drug allergies.

Family history: nil of note.

Social history

  • Never smoked. No recreational drugs.
  • Alcohol: 6 beers (full-strength cans) a day. Before the cirrhosis diagnosis it was 12 a day. Your last drink was at about 10 pm last night. You have never had a fit, seen things or been treated for withdrawal.
  • If asked CAGE-type questions: you are trying to cut down. You get annoyed when people ask about it (“it's part of my job”, client drinks and long nights). You feel very guilty about it. Sometimes you need a drink in the morning to steady yourself (an eye-opener).
  • Little exercise. Takeaway most nights.
  • You live alone.

Ideas, concerns and expectations

  • Idea: “My liver is acting up again.”
  • Concern: you can't focus, and you are worried you won't get back to work.
  • Expectation: to be patched up and back at work as soon as possible.
  • Question to raise once in Part 1: “Do I really have to stay in? I've got a big case on.” A good candidate acknowledges this and says they need to find out what is going on first.

The nurse and how Roger changes

  • If asked for observations, the nurse gives the triage set taken at 14:30: RR 18, SpO2 96% on room air, BP 108/64, HR 112 regular, temperature 38.6 °C, alert, pain 5/10, BGL 5.8 mmol/L. Weight 75 kg (measured at triage).
  • If asked for IV access and bloods: “Cannula's in and bloods are off, including a group and hold.” If asked for blood cultures: “Two sets taken.” If asked to tell a senior: “I'll let the registrar know.”
  • Partway through, the nurse says: “He's just had a really bad shivering episode, he was shaking all over.”
  • If the candidate orders medicines or a tap in Part 1, the examiner says: “Noted. Please cover your management in Part 2.” If they ask for results, say these come in Part 2.

Exam findings (give only when the candidate says what they are examining)

  • General: jaundiced, flushed, mildly uncomfortable, shivery. Alert and oriented. Thin arms and shoulders with a large abdomen.
  • Hands and arms: palmar erythema, leukonychia, no clubbing. Scratch marks (excoriations) on both forearms. Several bruises on the forearms. A fine tremor of the outstretched hands. No asterixis. Warm peripheries, CRT 2 seconds.
  • Face and neck: scleral icterus. Mucous membranes dry. No parotid enlargement. JVP not raised.
  • Chest: 5 spider naevi on the upper chest. Mild gynaecomastia. Heart sounds dual, no murmurs. Chest clear, no dullness at the bases.
  • Abdomen, inspection: distended with bulging flanks and an everted umbilicus. No scars. No caput medusae.
  • Abdomen, palpation: mild diffuse tenderness throughout. No guarding, no rigidity, no rebound tenderness. Liver not palpable. Spleen tip palpable on deep inspiration. No masses.
  • Percussion: dull in both flanks with shifting dullness present. Not tympanic.
  • Auscultation: bowel sounds present and normal.
  • Hernial orifices: no hernias.
  • Rectal examination (if requested, with a chaperone): brown stool, no melaena, no fresh blood, no mass.
  • Legs: pitting oedema to the ankles on both sides.
  • Mental state: oriented to time, place and person. Says the months of the year backwards without error.

check.x: Professionalism
Washes hands, introduces self, confirms Roger's identity and gains consent for the history and examination.
Recognises that a febrile, tachycardic patient with known cirrhosis may be septic, and during Part 1 asks the nurse for IV access, bloods with blood cultures, and to inform a senior.
check.d: The critical elements are blood cultures and senior notification, given in Part 1. Credit them whenever in Part 1 they are given.

check.x: Asks about alcohol without judgement, stays calm when Roger becomes defensive, and acknowledges his worry about work.
History
Characterises the pain:

kids.x: Site and radiation: whole abdomen, no radiation
Onset and duration: gradual, present on waking yesterday, getting worse
Character and modifying factors: constant ache, worse when pressing, nothing relieves it
Severity and impact: 4/10 rising to 5/10, cannot focus

check.x: Asks about infective symptoms and elicits fever, chills and night sweats since yesterday.
Elicits the features of liver decompensation:

kids.x: Jaundice and dark urine for 2 weeks

check.x: Asks specifically about hepatic encephalopathy (confusion, drowsiness) and GI bleeding (haematemesis, melaena or blood PR), all absent.
check.d: Both must be asked for the mark.

check.x: Screens with cluster questions for the other causes: pancreatitis (pain through to the back), bowel obstruction (vomiting, bowels, flatus), peptic ulcer (epigastric pain, NSAIDs), bowel cancer (weight loss, PR bleeding, change in bowel habit), biliary colic (pain after fatty meals), and extra-abdominal causes (chest pain, palpitations, urinary symptoms).
check.d: Score if at least 4 of the 6 clusters are screened.

check.x: Takes the past history: cirrhosis diagnosed 2 years ago with no follow-up, rarely sees doctors, no abdominal surgery, no known viral hepatitis (and asks about hepatitis risks).
Takes a medication and allergy history: paracetamol every other day for headaches, no NSAIDs or other medicines, no known drug allergies.
Takes a quantified alcohol history:
check.d: The critical elements are the amount and the time of the last drink (withdrawal risk).

kids.x: Amount now and before: 6 beers a day, 12 a day before the diagnosis
Dependence (CAGE or equivalent): trying to cut down, annoyed when asked, guilty, sometimes needs an eye-opener
Time of the last drink (10 pm last night)
Previous withdrawal: no fits or hallucinations

check.x: Takes the social and family history: non-smoker, no drugs, little exercise, takeaway most nights, lives alone, works as a lawyer; no relevant family history.
Explores his ideas, concerns and expectations: he thinks his liver is “acting up again”, cannot focus, and worries he won't get back to work.
Examination
Asks for the vital signs and notes the fever (38.6 °C) and tachycardia (HR 112) with a BP of 108/64; notes jaundice and that he is shivery.

Looks for the stigmata of chronic liver disease and identifies at least 4 (palmar erythema, leukonychia, excoriations, bruising, scleral icterus, spider naevi, gynaecomastia, muscle wasting, leg oedema).
check.d: Score if at least 4 are identified.

check.x: Assesses for hepatic encephalopathy and alcohol withdrawal: orientation and attention, asterixis (absent) and tremor (fine tremor present).
Examines the abdomen:
check.d: The critical elements are looking for peritonism and confirming ascites.

kids.x: Inspection: distension, bulging flanks, everted umbilicus, no scars or caput medusae
Palpation: mild diffuse tenderness, assesses for guarding, rigidity and rebound (all absent)
Palpates liver and spleen (spleen tip palpable), no masses
Percussion: flank dullness with shifting dullness, confirming ascites

check.x: Asks for a rectal examination for melaena (none), and examines the chest bases and legs (pitting ankle oedema) for other sources and fluid overload.
Interpretation

Interprets the observations: temperature in the yellow zone at triage; at 15:10 HR 122 and systolic BP 96 have also entered the yellow zone with a rigor, so he is septic and deteriorating, and the candidate escalates to a senior now (rapid response if any value turns red).
States that an ascitic neutrophil count of 1295 x10^6/L (250 or more) confirms spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, and that a Gram stain with no organisms does not exclude it (culture pending).
Interprets the rest of the ascitic fluid: SAAG ≥11 (calculated 20) = portal hypertensive ascites; no Runyon criteria for secondary peritonitis.
check.d: Credit listing the individual Runyon criteria (protein, glucose, LDH), but do not require it.

check.x: Interprets the bloods: infection markers (WCC/CRP), impaired synthetic function (bilirubin, albumin, INR) and presumed AKI (creatinine 118 vs 72); lactate 2.6.
check.d: The critical elements are the AKI and the impaired synthetic function. Credit Child-Pugh C but do not require it.

check.x: Gives the most likely diagnosis as spontaneous bacterial peritonitis with sepsis in decompensated alcohol-related cirrhosis, justified by fever, diffuse abdominal pain and worsening ascites in untreated cirrhosis with ongoing drinking, and the ascitic neutrophil count.

Gives at least 3 differentials, each with a feature for or against it from this case: secondary bacterial peritonitis, decompensated cirrhosis with ascites but no infection, acute pancreatitis, bowel obstruction, bowel cancer.
check.d: Also credit appendicitis, alcohol-related hepatitis, or early alcohol withdrawal as a contributor to the fever and tachycardia, with a reason. Credit citing the normal lipase against pancreatitis.

check.x: Management

Gives empirical IV antibiotics immediately after blood cultures (and the diagnostic tap, which must not delay them): the eTG sepsis regimen for an intra-abdominal source, e.g. piperacillin–tazobactam 4 g + 0.5 g IV 6-hourly (avoid gentamicin given cirrhosis and AKI), per local guideline and senior; ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily (eTG SBP regimen) also credited. If antibiotics were not ordered in Part 1, recognises that they are now overdue against the 60-minute sepsis target and gives them now.
check.d: Credit either regimen: the eTG or local sepsis regimen for an intra-abdominal source (e.g. piperacillin–tazobactam), or ceftriaxone or cefotaxime per eTG for SBP. The critical elements are cultures and prompt IV antibiotics. Also credit antibiotics ordered in Part 1.

check.x: Gives IV albumin to protect the kidneys: 1.5 g/kg within 6 hours (about 110 g of 20% albumin for 75 kg) and 1 g/kg on day 3.

Supports the kidneys and circulation: cautious fluid with reassessment, a fluid balance chart (with an IDC if needed) and daily UEC; avoids nephrotoxins (NSAIDs, aminoglycosides, IV contrast) and uses paracetamol at a reduced dose.
check.d: Score if at least 3 are given.

check.x: Gives IV thiamine before or with glucose (for example 300 mg IV daily) and starts alcohol withdrawal monitoring with symptom-triggered treatment on senior advice (a shorter-acting benzodiazepine such as oxazepam in liver disease).
Admits under gastroenterology or hepatology, asks for ICU review if hypotension persists, and involves the drug and alcohol team.
check.d: The critical elements are admission under gastroenterology or hepatology and escalation to ICU if hypotension persists. Credit drug and alcohol involvement but do not require it. Credit mention of long-term prophylaxis.

check.x: Explains to Roger in plain words and without judgement that the fluid in his tummy is infected because of his scarred liver, that he must stay in hospital for drip antibiotics and albumin, and that stopping alcohol is the most important thing for his liver; addresses his work worry honestly and checks his understanding.
Safety netting

Asks the nurses to report at once at least 3 of: confusion or drowsiness, vomiting blood or black stools, feeling faint or a falling BP, passing little urine, worsening pain, shakes, sweats or seeing things (withdrawal).
Tells Roger himself, in plain words, to call the nurse straight away if he feels muddled or drowsy, shaky or sees things, feels faint, vomits blood or the pain gets worse.

part2.lead: Here are Roger's observations, including the nurse's repeat set, his blood results, and the results of a diagnostic ascitic tap done by the ED registrar. [Examiner: if antibiotics were ordered in Part 1, say: “The antibiotic you charted was given at 15:15”, and add “after blood cultures” only if cultures were requested. The tap was done afterwards. Otherwise say: “No antibiotics have been given yet.”]
part2.patient:
When the examiner reads out your questions for question 4 (“Is it my liver acting up again? When can I get back to work?”), react to how the candidate answers:

  • If told he must stay in hospital: “Can't I just take tablets at home? I've got a trial next week.” Accept it if the candidate explains kindly why he needs drip treatment.
  • If the candidate raises the alcohol without judgement, admit: “I know. I feel terrible about it. I just don't know how to stop with my job.”
  • If the candidate lectures you, become defensive: “It's part of my job.”
  • If the candidate uses jargon (peritonitis, ascites, paracentesis, albumin), ask once: “What does that mean?”

handover.label: Observations
handover.result: Triage set at 14:30 and the nurse's repeat set at 15:10, both on room air. At 15:05 he had a rigor.
handover.model:
• Examiner note: the 15:10 pain score is blank. If analgesia was ordered in Part 1, tell the candidate it is 3/10 after analgesia; otherwise tell them it is 5/10 and none has been given. If antibiotics were ordered in Part 1, say: “The antibiotic you charted was given at 15:15”, and add “after blood cultures” only if cultures were requested. The tap was done afterwards. Otherwise say: “No antibiotics have been given yet.”
  • Read: at 14:30 the temperature of 38.6 °C is in the yellow zone; HR 112, BP 108/64, RR 18 and SpO2 96% are white. At 15:10, after a rigor, the temperature is 38.7 °C (yellow), HR 122 (yellow) and systolic BP 96 (yellow); RR, SpO2 and consciousness are white.
  • Meaning: fever with a rising heart rate and a falling BP after a rigor is sepsis with early hypotension. Patients with cirrhosis often have a low baseline BP, but this is a fall from 108 within 40 minutes, and the lactate is raised.
  • Changes: yellow zone values call for a clinical review within 30 minutes; in a septic cirrhotic patient do not wait: senior to the bedside now, antibiotics now if not already given (overdue; do not wait for the tap result), observations at least every 30 minutes, and a rapid response if systolic falls below 90 or any value turns red.

rows.note: Triage 14:30, ATS 2: febrile, generalised abdominal pain, known liver disease. Weight 75 kg (measured at triage)
Rigor at 15:05, looks more unwell. Doctor informed. Pain score: see examiner

handover.label: Blood results
handover.result: Roger Lee. Collected 14:35 at cannulation by the triage nurse. Sample not haemolysed. Previous result on file: creatinine 72 µmol/L (GP bloods at diagnosis, 2024). Hepatitis B and C serology sent, results to follow.
handover.model:
• Examiner note: if blood cultures were requested in Part 1, two sets were taken at 15:00, before any antibiotic; otherwise none have been taken.
  • Read: WCC 13.8 with neutrophils 11.6 and CRP 96. Hb 112 with MCV 104, platelets 78. Bilirubin 86, albumin 26, INR 1.9 (not anticoagulated). AST 132 more than twice ALT 58, GGT 380, ALP 168. Creatinine 118 against his last known value of 72 (2 years ago), urea 9.4. Na 129, K 3.4. Lactate 2.6. Lipase and glucose normal.
  • Meaning: an inflammatory response consistent with infection. Bilirubin, albumin, INR and low platelets show decompensated cirrhosis with impaired synthetic function and hypersplenism; with moderate ascites and no encephalopathy the Child-Pugh score is 12 (class C), credited but not required. Creatinine 118 is above range and 1.6 times his last known value (72, 2 years ago, so not a valid ICA baseline). Treat it as presumed AKI: in SBP this carries a high risk of hepatorenal syndrome, and muscle wasting means creatinine underestimates the loss of function. Albumin is given to prevent this. Lactate 2.6 with a falling BP means sepsis with hypoperfusion. Macrocytosis and the AST:ALT pattern fit alcohol. Normal lipase argues against pancreatitis.
  • Changes: albumin for the kidneys, avoid nephrotoxins, daily UEC; no FFP for the INR without bleeding; replace potassium; watch sodium.

labs.title: Full blood count, CRP and coagulation

handover.label: Diagnostic ascitic tap
handover.result:
Sample: diagnostic paracentesis by the ED registrar at 15:40, left iliac fossa, under bedside ultrasound guidance (moderate to large volume of free fluid; small, nodular liver). 40 mL withdrawn. 10 mL inoculated into each of an aerobic and an anaerobic blood culture bottle at the bedside; the rest sent for cell count, biochemistry and Gram stain.

Serum albumin at 14:35: 26 g/L.
handover.model:
• Read: cloudy fluid, white cells 1850 x10^6/L with neutrophils 70%, an absolute neutrophil count of 1295 x10^6/L. Total protein 9 g/L, albumin 6 g/L; the candidate calculates the SAAG as 26 − 6 = 20 g/L. Glucose 5.4 mmol/L (serum 5.8), LDH 112 U/L (below the serum upper limit of 250). Gram stain: neutrophils, no organisms. Culture pending.
  • Meaning: a neutrophil count of 250 x10^6/L or more in cirrhotic ascites is spontaneous bacterial peritonitis. The Gram stain is often negative and does not exclude it. SAAG of 11 or more means portal hypertensive ascites. Low protein (below 10 g/L) is a risk factor for SBP. None of the Runyon criteria for secondary peritonitis (protein above 10 g/L, glucose below 2.8 mmol/L, LDH above the serum upper limit) is met, so a perforation or abscess is less likely.
  • Changes: treat now with IV antibiotics and albumin; repeat the tap at 48 hours if he is not improving, and image for a surgical source if the neutrophil count does not fall or several organisms grow.

ask: You are now calling the gastroenterology registrar. Please give an ISBAR handover of Roger Lee, including your interpretation of these results.
What is your most likely diagnosis, and what else would you consider? Justify your answer.
Outline your management of Roger now, here in the emergency department.
Roger asks you, “Is it my liver acting up again? When can I get back to work?” Please answer him, then tell me what you would ask the nurses to watch for.
expect:
• Identify: self, ED intern; Roger Lee, 45.
  • Situation: spontaneous bacterial peritonitis with sepsis and presumed AKI; becoming hypotensive.
  • Background: alcohol-related cirrhosis diagnosed 2 years ago, no follow-up; 6 beers a day, last drink 10 pm; 2 weeks of distension, jaundice, dark urine, itch, bruising; fever, chills and diffuse pain since yesterday; paracetamol, NKDA.
  • Assessment: T 38.7, HR 122 and SBP 96 (now yellow zone, falling), lactate 2.6; WCC 13.8, CRP 96; creatinine 118 from 72 (presumed AKI); bilirubin 86, INR 1.9, albumin 26; platelets 78; lipase normal; ascitic neutrophils 1295 (≥250 = SBP), Gram stain no organisms (does not exclude, culture pending), SAAG 26 − 6 = 20 (portal hypertension), no Runyon criteria; no encephalopathy.
  • Recommendation: cultures, IV antibiotics and albumin given or charted; please review now for admission; ICU review if BP keeps falling.

Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis in decompensated alcohol-related cirrhosis: fever, chills, diffuse constant pain and worsening ascites; untreated cirrhosis with ongoing drinking; ascitic neutrophils 1295 (250 or more).

  • Secondary bacterial peritonitis (must not miss): for: fever, tenderness; against: no guarding or rigidity, protein 9, normal glucose and LDH, no organisms seen.
  • Decompensated cirrhosis with ascites, no infection: explains jaundice and swelling, not the fever or ascitic neutrophils.
  • Acute pancreatitis: for: alcohol; against: no back pain or vomiting, lipase normal.
  • Bowel obstruction: against: no vomiting, passing wind, no surgery, dull not tympanic.
  • Bowel cancer: against: no weight loss, PR bleeding or change in bowel habit.

1. Senior to the bedside now; sepsis pathway.
  2. Blood cultures (ascitic fluid already in culture bottles), then the eTG sepsis regimen for an intra-abdominal source, e.g. piperacillin–tazobactam 4 g + 0.5 g IV 6-hourly (avoid gentamicin given cirrhosis and AKI), per local guideline and senior; ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily (eTG SBP regimen) also credited. Antibiotics now if not already given (overdue; do not wait for the tap result).
  3. IV albumin 1.5 g/kg within 6 hours (about 110 g), 1 g/kg on day 3.
  4. Cautious fluid with reassessment; fluid balance (IDC if needed); daily UEC; no NSAIDs, aminoglycosides or IV contrast; reduced-dose paracetamol; replace potassium.
  5. IV thiamine (e.g. 300 mg) before glucose; withdrawal scale with symptom-triggered oxazepam on senior advice; watch for encephalopathy.
  6. Admit under gastroenterology or hepatology; ICU if hypotension persists; repeat tap at 48 hours if not improving; drug and alcohol team.

• Plain words, no judgement: the scarred liver has let fluid build up and that fluid is infected; it is serious but treatable with drip antibiotics and albumin; he must stay in hospital for some days, so work has to wait; stopping alcohol completely is the most important thing for his liver; offers drug and alcohol support; tells him to call the nurse straight away if he feels muddled, shaky, faint or vomits blood; checks understanding.
  • Nurses report at once (at least 3): confusion or drowsiness, vomiting blood or black stools, faintness or falling BP, little urine, worse pain, shakes, sweats or seeing things.

ddx.dx: Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis in decompensated alcohol-related cirrhosis
ddx.for: Fever, chills and constant diffuse abdominal pain since yesterday with ascites growing over 2 weeks, in untreated alcohol-related cirrhosis with ongoing drinking, and an ascitic neutrophil count of 1295 x10^6/L.

ddx.dx: Secondary bacterial peritonitis (perforated viscus or intra-abdominal abscess)
ddx.for: Fever, generalised abdominal tenderness and neutrophils in the ascitic fluid.
ddx.against: Gradual onset, no guarding or rigidity, no previous surgery, ascitic protein 9 g/L, glucose 5.4 mmol/L and LDH below the serum limit, and no organisms on Gram stain.

ddx.dx: Decompensated cirrhosis with ascites but no infection
ddx.for: Two weeks of jaundice, dark urine, itch, bruising and swelling, with bilirubin 86, albumin 26, INR 1.9 and a SAAG of 20 g/L.
ddx.against: It does not explain the fever, rigors, WCC 13.8 or the ascitic neutrophil count.

ddx.for: Heavy daily drinking with constant abdominal pain.
ddx.against: The pain is generalised, not epigastric through to the back, there is no vomiting, and lipase is 40 U/L.
No vomiting, bowels opening and passing wind, constant not colicky pain, no previous surgery, normal bowel sounds and dull rather than tympanic percussion.

ddx.for: Abdominal distension at 45 with a poor diet and heavy alcohol use.
ddx.against: No weight loss, PR bleeding or change in bowel habit, and the swelling is portal hypertensive ascites with a SAAG of 20 g/L.

guide:
In Part 1, Roger gives each part of the history only when asked, and the examiner gives findings from the Exam findings only when the candidate says what they are examining. The nurse reports the rigor partway through. If the candidate orders treatment or a tap in Part 1, say “Noted, please cover it in Part 2”, and credit an early antibiotic order under item 30; mark early instructions to the nurse (cultures, senior notification) under Professionalism. If they ask for results, say they will come in Part 2. In Part 2, hand over the observations, bloods and ascitic tap results. If antibiotics were ordered in Part 1, say: “The antibiotic you charted was given at 15:15”, and add “after blood cultures” only if cultures were requested. The tap was done afterwards. Otherwise say: “No antibiotics have been given yet.” If blood cultures were requested in Part 1, two sets were taken at 15:00, before any antibiotic; otherwise none have been taken. Then ask all four questions in order. The 15:10 pain score is blank: give it as 3/10 if analgesia was ordered in Part 1, otherwise 5/10 with none given. Read out Roger's questions to open question 4. He reacts while the candidate answers.

A high-performing candidate sees a septic patient with cirrhosis from the triage observations and asks for cultures and a senior early. They characterise the pain, elicit the fever and the 2 weeks of decompensation, and rule out encephalopathy and GI bleeding. They screen the other differentials in clusters and quantify the alcohol with CAGE and the time of the last drink. They examine for stigmata, asterixis, peritonism and shifting dullness. In Part 2 they read the ascitic neutrophil count as SBP and the creatinine rise as presumed AKI. They spot the deteriorating yellow zone observations, give antibiotics and albumin at the right doses, give thiamine, plan withdrawal monitoring, admit, and explain to Roger without judgement.

A borderline candidate takes the pain history but misses the fever or the alcohol quantity, does not examine for ascites, or calls it “just decompensation”. They may give antibiotics without albumin, miss the AKI, give NSAIDs for pain, forget thiamine, or agree that Roger can go home.
explain:
Diagnosis: spontaneous bacterial peritonitis

Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP) is infection of ascitic fluid without an intra-abdominal surgical source. It occurs almost only in cirrhosis with ascites. The classic triad is fever, diffuse abdominal pain and worsening ascites. The pain is often mild, because the ascites separates the inflamed peritoneal surfaces, and some patients have no symptoms at all. Untreated, it progresses to shock, hepatorenal syndrome and multi-organ failure. Roger fits the picture: fever, chills and constant generalised pain since yesterday, on top of 2 weeks of worsening ascites, jaundice, dark urine, itch and bruising. These are signs of decompensated alcohol-related cirrhosis that has gone untreated since he was lost to follow-up 2 years ago. Low ascitic protein (below 10 g/L) and advanced liver disease (Child-Pugh C) are the main risk factors.

Taking the history

Use reading time to list the causes of generalised abdominal pain in a heavy drinker, then ask in clusters: infection (fever, chills), decompensation (swelling, jaundice, itch, bruising), encephalopathy (confusion), GI bleeding (haematemesis, melaena), pancreatitis, obstruction, peptic ulcer, bowel cancer, biliary colic, and extra-abdominal causes. Quantify the alcohol, screen for dependence (CAGE) and record the last drink, because withdrawal can begin within hours of admission. Roger's eye-opener shows physical dependence.

Differentials

  • Secondary bacterial peritonitis (perforation or abscess) needs surgery and must not be missed. Suspect it with peritonism, several organisms on Gram stain or culture, or ascitic fluid meeting two Runyon criteria: protein above 10 g/L, glucose below 2.8 mmol/L, LDH above the serum upper limit. If suspected, arrange a CT.
  • Decompensated cirrhosis without infection explains the ascites and jaundice but not the fever or ascitic neutrophils. Every patient with cirrhosis and ascites admitted to hospital, or with fever, pain, encephalopathy, AKI or a GI bleed, needs a diagnostic tap.
  • Pancreatitis, bowel obstruction, bowel cancer and appendicitis are less likely on the history and examination.
  • Alcohol-related hepatitis can also cause fever, jaundice and a raised white cell count in a heavy drinker and may coexist; it does not explain the ascitic neutrophils.
  • Early alcohol withdrawal (last drink about 17 hours ago, fine tremor) can add to the fever and tachycardia but does not explain the ascitic neutrophils; treat both.

Interpreting the results

  • Ascitic fluid: a neutrophil count of 250 x10^6/L (per mm³) or more is diagnostic. Culture is negative in many cases, so treatment does not wait for it. Inoculating blood culture bottles at the bedside improves the yield. The SAAG is calculated as serum albumin minus ascitic albumin (26 − 6 = 20 g/L); 11 g/L or more confirms portal hypertensive ascites.
  • Bloods: bilirubin, albumin, INR and platelets show decompensated cirrhosis. Bilirubin above 51 µmol/L, albumin below 28, INR 1.7 to 2.3 and moderate ascites (3 points) without encephalopathy give a Child-Pugh score of 12 (class C). Creatinine 118 is 1.6 times his last known value of 72, but that value is 2 years old and not a valid baseline, so treat it as presumed AKI, an early warning of hepatorenal syndrome, which complicates a large share of SBP episodes. Muscle wasting means creatinine underestimates the loss of kidney function. Hyponatraemia, macrocytosis and AST more than twice ALT fit cirrhosis and alcohol.
  • Observations: on the NSW Between the Flags chart his fever is yellow zone at triage. Forty minutes later his heart rate and systolic BP are yellow too, and with a lactate of 2.6 this is sepsis with hypoperfusion. Escalate to a senior now.

Management

  • Antibiotics: after blood cultures, start empirical IV antibiotics without waiting for culture. Ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily (or cefotaxime) is the eTG regimen for SBP without sepsis. Roger has sepsis with hypoperfusion, so follow the eTG regimen for sepsis or septic shock with an intra-abdominal source (for example piperacillin–tazobactam 4 g + 0.5 g IV 6-hourly), or the local sepsis pathway, and avoid aminoglycosides because of his cirrhosis and AKI. Discuss with the senior. The ACSQHC Sepsis Clinical Care Standard asks for antibiotics within 60 minutes when sepsis is recognised. Healthcare-associated infection or recent antibiotics may need broader cover. Rationalise to the culture result.
  • Albumin: 20% albumin 1.5 g/kg within 6 hours of diagnosis and 1 g/kg on day 3. It reduces renal failure and death in SBP.
  • Protect the kidneys: avoid NSAIDs, aminoglycosides and IV contrast where possible, hold diuretics, monitor fluid balance and check UEC daily. Do not correct the INR with FFP unless he is bleeding.
  • Analgesia: paracetamol at a reduced maximum dose in liver disease, avoid NSAIDs, and use opioids cautiously (they can precipitate encephalopathy).
  • Alcohol: IV thiamine before or with glucose to prevent Wernicke encephalopathy. Monitor with a withdrawal scale and give symptom-triggered treatment, preferring a shorter-acting benzodiazepine such as oxazepam in decompensated liver disease, on senior advice. Watch for encephalopathy and treat it with lactulose if it develops.
  • Response: repeat the tap at 48 hours if he is not improving. A neutrophil count that does not fall by at least a quarter suggests treatment failure or a secondary cause.
  • Disposition: admit under gastroenterology or hepatology, ICU if hypotension persists, with the drug and alcohol team and social work involved early.

After the episode

After one episode of SBP the risk of recurrence is high, so he needs long-term secondary prophylaxis (for example trimethoprim with sulfamethoxazole daily, as eTG advises). Other steps:

  • Hepatology follow-up, including referral for transplant assessment where appropriate.
  • Gastroscopy to screen for varices.
  • 6-monthly liver ultrasound for hepatocellular carcinoma.
  • Hepatitis serology and vaccination.
  • A low-salt diet and diuretics for the ascites once his kidneys recover.
  • Abstinence support, which is the single most important step for his prognosis.

Safety netting

In hospital, the nurses and Roger report confusion or drowsiness, bleeding, faintness, low urine output, worsening pain or withdrawal symptoms at once. After discharge he returns to the ED for fever, worsening pain or swelling, confusion, yellowing or black stools, and calls 000 for vomiting blood or collapse. He should see his GP within a week of discharge.
points: Fever, abdominal pain, worsening ascites, encephalopathy, AKI or a GI bleed in a patient with cirrhosis and ascites call for a diagnostic ascitic tap. SBP can be painless.
An ascitic neutrophil count of 250 x10^6/L (per mm³) or more is diagnostic of SBP. Inoculate blood culture bottles at the bedside and do not wait for the culture result.

Treat with prompt IV antibiotics as eTG recommends (ceftriaxone for SBP without sepsis; the sepsis regimen for an intra-abdominal source when the patient is septic), and give IV albumin (1.5 g/kg within 6 hours, 1 g/kg on day 3) to prevent hepatorenal syndrome.
Look for secondary peritonitis: peritonism, several organisms, or Runyon criteria (protein above 10 g/L, glucose below 2.8 mmol/L, LDH above the serum limit).
Quantify alcohol with the last drink, give thiamine before glucose and monitor for withdrawal. Avoid NSAIDs and nephrotoxins in cirrhosis.
After an episode, start long-term antibiotic prophylaxis and arrange hepatology follow-up, variceal screening, HCC surveillance and alcohol support.
